endorsements.quote: Recognizing distinct information needs and varying health and technical literacy among users and clinicians, our single facts label provides a layered approach with essential, comprehendible information at its primary level, designed for a 6th-grade equivalent reading level ( 37 , 39 , 40 ), and more clinically and technically detailed information separately accessible, ensuring both user approachability and clinician depth.
Risks and limitations This section elaborates on appropriateness by identifying risks, drawing on model development information to ensure accountability.

unlisted_practices: AI mental health technology developers should adopt a standardized facts label communicating intended use, warnings, risks and limitations, model information, clinical evidence, accessibility and usability, and privacy and security to clinicians and patients.
Developers should state whether an AI mental health technology is appropriate for use during a crisis and identify fallback resources when a crisis falls outside the tool's scope.
Developers should disclose whether an AI mental health technology is appropriate for individuals with serious mental illness and for children.
Developers should update the facts label as models evolve, treating it as a living document.
Regulators should require AI digital mental health technology developers to maintain transparency using a standardized facts label framework.
Developers should disclose whether clinicians and individuals with lived experience were involved in developing the AI tool.
Developers should disclose accessibility features and usability testing, including cultural, visual, cognitive, digital literacy, and internet requirements.
Developers should disclose the clinical research basis for the AI tool, explicitly stating when none exists.
Future work should empirically evaluate the usability and effectiveness of the facts label through usability testing and co-design with patients, caregivers, advocacy groups, and developers.

screen.reason: The paper proposes a governance and risk communication framework (a standardized facts label for AI-enabled digital mental health technologies) developed by an expert committee, rather than an empirical evaluation.
